title: Aiming line
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The aiming line shows the direction of your current shot. Change your aim and watch the line move across the table. Use it to explore how small adjustments change the intended contact with an object ball.

title: Ghost ball
text: The ghost ball shows the cue-ball position needed at contact to send an object ball toward the chosen pocket. Use it as an aiming reference, then adjust the shot and examine the result.

title: Tangent line
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The tangent line helps you study the cue ball’s initial direction after an angled collision when it arrives sliding without forward or backward roll. Follow and draw can change the path that develops afterward.

title: Diamond references
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The diamonds around the rails provide reference points for planning bank and kick shots. Compare the route you expect with the shot simulation, then adjust the aiming point as needed.

title: Trajectory guides
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Trajectory guides help you visualize possible ball paths. Change the aim, speed, or spin and notice how the ball movement changes. Use them to compare different shot choices.

title: Pocket targeting
text: Choose the pocket you want to approach, then use the aiming references to study the required object-ball path. A different pocket can change the cut angle and the cue-ball position you create.

title: Physics and calibration overview
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Physics and Calibration lets you explore how table and ball behavior affects a shot. Rolling friction and sliding friction are among the settings available. Adjust a parameter, repeat a shot, and compare the outcome.

title: Banks and kicks
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: In a bank shot, the object ball rebounds from a cushion on its way toward a pocket. In a kick shot, the cue ball contacts a cushion before reaching the object ball. Use the rail and diamond references to explore both routes.

title: Hide Cue Ball 1 and Cue Ball 2
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: When planning two shots, the aiming lines and guides can overlap. Select Hide Cue Ball 1 or Hide Cue Ball 2 to temporarily clear that shot’s visual guides. This lets you focus on the other shot while making adjustments. Select Show to bring the hidden guides back.

title: Shot speed
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Use shot speed to explore how strongly the cue ball travels. Start at a moderate speed, execute the shot, then restore the arrangement and try a small adjustment. Notice where the cue ball finishes.

title: Fine speed adjustment
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: For small speed changes, use the available fine-adjustment controls. On a computer, you can also hover over the speed control and use the mouse wheel. Compare the result after each adjustment.

title: Jump height
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: For a jump shot, examine how high the cue ball rises along its path. The maximum height is not necessarily the height at the obstacle, so check the trajectory where the obstacle actually sits.

title: Obstacle clearance
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: When attempting to jump an obstructing ball, examine the cue-ball path at the obstacle’s location. A shot clears the obstacle only if the cue ball is high enough at that point, not simply because it reaches a high point elsewhere.

title: Landing point
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The predicted landing point shows where the airborne cue ball returns to the cloth. Compare landing position as you change elevation and speed, then consider how the cue ball may continue moving after it lands.

title: Massé shot controls
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: A mass-ay shot uses cue elevation and off-center spin to create a curved cue-ball path. Explore the curve by changing one setting at a time, and compare it with a cushion route around the same obstacle.

title: Direct cue-tip contact
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The cue-ball diagram is interactive. Click or touch the ball to position the red cue-tip contact marker. Move above center for follow, below center for draw, or to either side for English. Combine directions to explore different spin settings.

title: C and P power meters
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The two meters beside the cue-ball diagram show power along the shot. C is the cue ball’s power reaching the object ball. P is the object ball’s power toward the pocket. The white horizontal line marks the power needed at each stage. If a meter is well below that line, the shot may not have enough power to reach its intended destination.

title: Power meter
text: Set up a straight shot and gradually reduce shot speed until one power meter falls below the white line. Increase speed a little at a time and watch the C and P readings. Find a speed that supplies enough power while keeping the cue ball under control.

title: Opening 3D jump and massé controls
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Select 3D Jump / mass-ay Features to open the cue-elevation controls and side-view diagram. Adjust the cue angle with the slider, minus or plus buttons, or by entering a number directly. The side view shows the cue stick, red tip-contact point, and gold ball center.

title: Cue elevation for advanced shots
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Ordinary strokes use a cue close to level. Jump and mass-ay shots use considerably greater elevation. For a jump, explore elevation and speed to lift the cue ball over an obstacle. For mass-ay, combine elevation and off-center tip contact to bend the cue-ball path. Use the side view together with the overhead route.

title: Contact point
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The contact point is where the cue ball touches the object ball. Changing that point changes the direction the object ball travels. Use the visual guides to compare the contact point with the pocket you want to reach.

title: Cut angle
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: A cut shot sends the object ball away from the cue ball’s incoming direction. As the cut becomes thinner, the required contact point moves farther toward the edge of the object ball. Compare several angles and observe the change.

title: Ball overlap
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Ball overlap describes how much of the object ball the cue ball covers along the aiming line. A fuller hit has more overlap, while a thinner cut has less. Use overlap as another way to understand the contact angle.

title: Ghost-ball position
text: Imagine the cue ball at the instant it contacts the object ball. The ghost-ball guide shows that position. For balls of equal size, the centers are one ball diameter apart at contact. Aim through that position to study the intended object-ball path.

title: Collision line
text: The collision line connects the centers of the two balls at impact. For an ideal collision, the object ball initially moves along this line. Use it to see why even a small change in contact position can change the shot.

title: The tangent line
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: For a cut shot with a sliding cue ball, the cue ball initially leaves the collision close to a line perpendicular to the object ball’s path. This is the tangent line. Follow and draw can bend the cue ball away from that initial direction.

title: Bank-shot geometry
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: A bank shot sends the object ball to a cushion before it reaches a pocket. Start by identifying the intended rail contact point, then compare the incoming and outgoing paths. Speed, spin, and cushion response can change the rebound.

title: Kick-shot geometry
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: A kick shot sends the cue ball into a cushion before contacting an object ball. Study the cue ball’s route to the rail and its route away from the rail. Use the diamond references to help estimate where to aim.

title: Diamond references
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The diamonds along the rails provide repeatable reference points for planning banks and kicks. Use them to compare aiming lines and rail contact points. With practice, they can help you recognize useful routes across the table.

title: Mirror aiming
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: One way to visualize a simple bank is to imagine the target reflected across the cushion. Draw a line toward that reflected target to estimate a rail contact point. Then use the trainer to see how the cushion changes the actual path.

title: Choosing the rail contact point
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: For a bank or kick, identify where the moving ball should meet the cushion. Adjust the aim and execute the shot, then compare the actual rebound with your intended route. Small changes at the rail can create large differences farther down the table.

title: English off a cushion
text: Left or right English can change how the cue ball rebounds from a cushion. Set up the same rail shot without sidespin, then repeat it with left and right English. Compare the outgoing paths rather than assuming every rail behaves the same.

title: Multiple-rail routes
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Some shots use two or more cushions to reach a target. Break the route into individual rail contacts and study each change in direction. Start with a simple two-rail path before experimenting with more complicated routes.

title: Geometry practice challenge
text: Set up an object ball with a clear pocketing route. First study a direct shot, then arrange a bank shot and a kick shot to reach a target. Compare the aiming references and cushion paths. Restore the layout between attempts so the differences are easier to observe.

title: Positioning the cue ball
text: Move the cue ball to choose your starting position. Notice how the aiming line and available shots change as you reposition it. Try several starting points before deciding which shot to practice.

title: Creating a simple practice layout
text: Begin with the cue ball and one object ball. Choose a pocket, adjust their positions, and execute the shot. Once that feels comfortable, add a second object ball and plan where the cue ball should finish.

title: Pocketed-ball tracking
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: As balls are pocketed, the table changes. Watch which balls remain available and adjust your plan to fit the new arrangement. The important question is not only which ball went in, but what opportunity the shot created.

title: Exercise: change one ball
text: Set up a simple cut shot and execute it. Restore the starting arrangement, then move the object ball slightly while keeping the cue ball in place. Adjust your aim and execute again. Notice how the contact point and required cut angle change.

title: Exercise: build and review a rack
text: Choose a rack or create a multi-ball layout. Work through your planned sequence, extending Shot 2 as you go. When you finish, use Undo Last Shot to move backward through the rack and identify one positional decision you could improve.

title: — save, change, and recall
text: Set up a simple shot and save the layout with a name you will recognize. Move one of the balls to create a different shot. Now open Save / Recall Layout, select your saved arrangement, and load it. Compare the restored setup with your original practice shot.

title: Table Speed
text: Position the cue ball with an unobstructed path. Choose a moderate shot speed and execute the shot. Observe how far the ball travels before stopping. Restore the starting position, then open Physics & Calibration and adjust the rolling friction setting. Execute Shot again using the same speed. Compare the distances and notice how rolling friction influences table speed.

title: Physics and Calibration overview
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Physics & Calibration starts with carefully tested defaults that work well right out of the box. You can practice without changing anything. Advanced controls are there when you want to fine-tune a particular table or study the physics in more detail.

title: What calibration can and cannot do
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The default calibration settings have been carefully tested and are ready for practice. Advanced calibration is available when you want to explore individual physical settings or fine-tune the trainer for a particular table.

title: Rolling friction and table speed
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Rolling friction influences how quickly a rolling ball slows down. Lower rolling resistance generally allows the ball to travel farther. Higher rolling resistance generally shortens its travel. Compare identical shots after each adjustment.

title: Sliding friction
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Sliding friction affects how a ball changes from sliding to rolling. It also influences how long backspin or forward spin persists while the cue ball travels. Compare stop, follow, and draw shots to see the difference.

title: Shot speed and distance
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Shot speed determines how much motion you give the cue ball. Use the same layout and change only the speed control. Execute Shot after each adjustment and compare both the cue ball and object ball travel.

title: Cue ball collisions
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: When the cue ball strikes an object ball, the collision changes the direction and speed of both balls. The contact point matters: a full hit behaves differently from a thin cut. Use the guides to compare their paths.

title: Collision energy and restitution
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Ball collisions do not transfer energy perfectly. Restitution describes how strongly balls separate after contact. Small changes in collision behavior can affect object-ball travel and the cue ball’s remaining speed.

title: Follow through contact
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Forward rotation can carry the cue ball beyond the contact point after it strikes an object ball. Try a straight shot with moderate follow, then compare it with the same shot using less forward rotation.

title: Draw through contact
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Backspin can make the cue ball return after contact, especially on a nearly straight shot. Repeat the same layout while adjusting draw and speed. Watch whether the cue ball still has backspin when it reaches the object ball.

title: Stop and stun
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: A stun shot reaches the object ball while the cue ball is sliding, with little forward or backward rotation. On a straight, full hit, this can produce a stop shot. On a cut, the cue ball initially follows the tangent line.

title: Side spin or English
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Left and right English change how the cue ball interacts with cushions and can influence its route after contact. Compare shots with no English, then left English, then right English, keeping other settings the same.

title: Spin transfer
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Friction at ball-to-ball contact can transfer some rotational influence during a collision. The effect is usually smaller than the primary change in direction caused by the contact geometry, but it can matter on certain shots.

title: Cue ball deflection or squirt
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Striking the cue ball away from its vertical center can change its initial direction. This effect is often called squirt or cue-ball deflection. Compare the aiming line and predicted route when you add side spin.

title: Swerve and cloth interaction
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: With cue elevation and side spin, the cue ball can curve as it travels over the cloth. This is called swerve. Its amount depends on speed, elevation, spin, and the frictional interaction with the cloth.

title: Rail speed loss
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Cushion contact generally reduces ball speed. The exact rebound also depends on the cushion’s response and the ball’s rotation. Multiple-rail routes compound these effects, so compare them at consistent speeds.

title: Jump trajectory
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: For a jump shot, look at the height of the cue ball along its route. A useful jump must rise high enough at the obstacle and land in a workable area. Adjust elevation, speed, and tip contact to compare results.

title: Clearing an obstacle
text: Place an object ball between the cue ball and your target. As you change the jump settings, check the cue ball’s predicted height where it crosses the obstacle. A path that passes over the ball is different from one that collides with it.

title: Landing position
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The landing point matters as much as clearing the obstacle. A jump that lands too early can strike the blocking ball, while a late landing can make the next contact difficult. Compare the landing position before selecting Execute Shot.

title: Understanding jump trajectory
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Use the jump trajectory to study how cue elevation, tip contact, and speed affect the height and landing point of the cue ball.

title: Massé shot
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: A mass-ay shot uses elevated cue delivery and off-center spin to curve the cue ball around an obstacle. Explore how elevation, side spin, and speed change the curve. These shots are sensitive, so make small adjustments.

title: Massé versus jump
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: A jump route aims to carry the cue ball above an obstacle. A mass-ay route bends the ball’s path around it through elevated, off-center contact and interaction with the cloth. Compare clearance and landing for a jump with lateral curvature for a mass-ay.

title: Table dimensions and ball geometry
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Accurate table and ball dimensions help the aiming guides match the layout. If you adjust a geometry setting, verify it against the table you are trying to model before interpreting small differences in a shot.

title: Reading physical measurements
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Use the displayed measurements as guides to the simulated shot. When height or clearance is shown in inches, compare the values with the ball’s approximate size and the space available around an obstacle.

title: Calibrating against a real table
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Choose a simple repeatable shot on a real table. Match the starting ball positions in the trainer, execute the shot, and compare where the balls stop. Adjust one relevant calibration setting, then try again.

title: Change one variable at a time
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: To understand a result, change only one control between attempts. If you change speed, spin, and friction together, you will not know which change caused the difference. Keep the layout and other settings consistent.

title: Save your calibration observations
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: As you compare simulated and real shots, keep a simple record of the layout, shot speed, spin, and calibration settings. Note what improved and what did not. Repeatable observations are more useful than a single lucky match.

title: table speed
text: Position the cue ball with an unobstructed path. Choose a moderate shot speed and execute the shot. Observe how far the ball travels before stopping. Restore the starting position, then open Physics & Calibration and adjust the rolling friction setting. Execute Shot again using the same speed. Compare the distances and notice how rolling friction influences table speed.

title: sliding friction
text: Set up a straight shot and use the same shot speed each time. Compare a stop shot with a follow shot, then adjust sliding friction and repeat. Observe how the cue ball’s behavior changes as it approaches and passes the object ball.

title: speed ladder
text: Place the cue ball on a clear path. Execute Shot at a low speed, restore the position, then repeat at medium and higher speeds. Compare stopping distances. Try to predict the next distance before running each shot.

title: stop, follow, draw
text: Use one straight-shot layout. First attempt a stop shot, then restore the layout for a follow shot, and finally try draw. Change only the relevant spin and speed controls. Compare the cue ball’s path after impact.

title: rail and English
text: Aim the cue ball toward a cushion at a moderate angle. Execute Shot with no English, then repeat with left English and right English. Compare the rebound directions while keeping the starting position and speed unchanged.

title: squirt comparison
text: Choose a long, nearly straight shot. Start with center-ball contact, then add left or right English. Observe any change in the initial cue-ball direction. Adjust the aim and compare the resulting contact point.

title: jump clearance
text: Place a blocking ball between the cue ball and your target. Adjust elevation and speed until the trajectory clears the blocker. Check the landing point as well, then execute the shot and review the result.

title: jump landing
text: Set up a jump over an obstacle with open cloth beyond it. Choose a desired landing area. Change one jump setting at a time and compare the landing point. Try to clear the obstacle while landing as close as possible to the chosen area.

title: massé route
text: Arrange a blocking ball so a direct path is unavailable. Experiment with cue elevation and side spin to create a mass-ay route around it. Compare the curve at several speeds, then execute a promising shot.

title: real-table comparison
text: Choose a simple shot you can repeat on a real table. Record the starting positions and approximate stopping points. Recreate the arrangement in the trainer, execute the shot, and compare. Adjust one calibration setting and repeat to see whether the match improves.

title: Table and ball geometry settings
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Open Physics / Calibration to set the playing length, width, and ball diameter in inches. Choose a table-size preset when appropriate, or enter the dimensions of the table you are studying.

title: Surface and collision settings
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Sliding friction affects how the cue ball transitions from sliding to rolling. Rolling friction influences how far balls travel. Ball-to-ball friction, restitution, rail rebound, and rail tangential damping let you study collision and cushion behavior.

title: Advanced jump physics settings
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Physics / Calibration also contains the 3D jump, mass-ay, and airborne physics setting, along with bed vertical restitution and bed impact friction. Use these settings to study elevated shots and how the cue ball interacts with the table surface.

title: Full Rack Runout Analysis
text: Set up a full rack and work through your planned runout. Use Shot 2 to continually extend your sequence as each shot is executed. After completing the rack, use Undo Last Shot repeatedly to travel backward through your entire shot history. Find a shot where better cue-ball positioning could have simplified the runout. Adjust that shot and explore an improved sequence from that point forward.

title: Practicing with Shot 2
text: Plan your first shot, then add Shot 2 to examine the next opportunity. Execute Shot to complete the first stroke. The second planned cue ball becomes the active cue ball. Before continuing, you can add another Shot 2 to extend your plan. This allows you to build a longer sequence, one shot at a time.

title: Practicing with Undo Last Shot
text: Undo Last Shot lets you revisit previous shots in your sequence. You can work backward through an entire rack, one shot at a time. Use this feature to identify a difficult position, return to the shot that created it, and explore a better approach before continuing.

title: The Three-Ball Runout
text: Place three object balls on the table and choose your pocketing order. Plan Shot 1 and Shot 2, then execute the first shot. Add another Shot 2 before continuing. Complete the three-ball sequence, then use Undo Last Shot to revisit any position you would like to improve.

title: Full-Rack Runout Review
text: Begin with a full rack and plan your runout. Use Shot 2 to continually extend the sequence as you execute each shot. When you've finished, use Undo Last Shot to work backward through the rack. Identify an earlier position that could have been improved, adjust the shot, and explore a better route through the remaining balls.

title: Jump, Kick, or Massé
text: Place an obstacle between the cue ball and the target ball. First, explore a kick shot using a cushion. Next, examine a mass-ay shot, using cue elevation and sidespin to curve the cue ball around the obstacle. Finally, investigate a jump shot that carries the cue ball over the obstacle. Compare the three techniques and consider which offers the best control.

title: The Runout Improvement Challenge
text: Choose a rack or practice layout and work through the complete sequence. After finishing, use Undo Last Shot to review your decisions. Find an earlier shot where a different cue-ball position could have improved the remaining pattern. Change that shot and work forward again. Repeat until you develop a more comfortable and reliable runout.

title: Managing cue-ball traffic
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: A crowded table creates obstacles for the cue ball. Before choosing a route, look at the other balls and consider where the cue ball can travel safely. Sometimes a short, controlled path is better than a longer route that passes through several obstacles.

title: Planning a defensive cue-ball route
text: When planning a safety, decide where you want the cue ball to finish. Look for areas where another ball blocks a direct route to the target. Then explore the speed and contact angle needed to move the cue ball into that area. Use the trainer to study the geometry before executing the shot.

title: Learning to aim accurately
text: Begin with a simple straight shot. Place the cue ball and object ball in line with a pocket. Use the aiming guides to examine the contact point, then select Execute Shot. Once you're comfortable, move the cue ball slightly to create a cut angle. Repeat with progressively more difficult angles.

title: Developing speed control
text: Speed control determines where the cue ball finishes. Set up a shot with a clear path and choose a stopping area. Execute Shot and observe the result. Restore the arrangement, make a small speed adjustment, and try again. Your goal is to learn how different stroke speeds affect travel distance.

title: Understanding stop shots
text: A stop shot occurs when the cue ball strikes an object ball straight on while sliding without forward or backward rotation. Ideally, the cue ball stops near the collision point as the object ball moves away. Experiment with speed and spin to learn how to create this result.

title: Practicing follow shots
text: Set up a straight shot and apply forward rotation to the cue ball. Execute Shot and observe how the cue ball continues after contacting the object ball. Repeat with different amounts of follow and speed. Try to control how far the cue ball travels beyond the contact point.

title: Practicing draw shots
text: Set up a straight shot and apply backspin. Execute Shot and observe whether the cue ball returns toward its starting position. Adjust the amount of draw and shot speed, then repeat. Try to bring the cue ball back to a specific area of the table.

title: Practicing cut angles
text: Place an object ball near the center of the table and select a pocket. Move the cue ball to create different cut angles. Use the ghost-ball guide to study the required contact point, then execute each shot. Compare how the aiming position changes as the cut becomes thinner.

title: Practicing the tangent line
text: Set up a cut shot and examine the tangent-line guide. Try a stun shot so the cue ball is sliding when it contacts the object ball. Execute Shot and observe the cue ball's initial direction after impact. Repeat with different cut angles to develop a feel for the tangent line.

title: Practicing bank shots
text: Choose an object ball and a pocket that requires a bank shot. Use the cushion and diamond references to estimate the rail contact point. Execute Shot and observe the rebound. Adjust your aim and speed, then repeat until you develop a more consistent banking approach.

title: Practicing kick shots
text: A kick shot sends the cue ball into a cushion before it contacts the object ball. Place an object ball where a direct shot is difficult. Use the diamond references to plan a one-rail route, then execute the shot. Experiment with the rail contact point and speed to improve your accuracy.

title: Practicing English
text: Set up a shot where the cue ball will contact a cushion. Begin without sidespin and observe the rebound. Restore the arrangement and add left English, then right English. Compare the results and notice how sidespin changes the cue ball's path.

title: Practicing cue-ball position
text: Place two object balls on the table and choose the order you want to pocket them. Before executing the first shot, decide where the cue ball should finish for the second. Use speed and spin to explore different routes. Your goal is to create a comfortable next shot, not simply pocket the first ball.

title: The Straight-Shot Ladder
text: Begin with the cue ball and object ball aligned toward a pocket. Execute the shot, then restore the arrangement. Gradually increase the distance between the balls while keeping the shot straight. Repeat at several distances, paying attention to aiming accuracy and shot speed.

title: Stop, Follow, Draw
text: Set up a straight shot. First, adjust the stroke to produce a stop shot. Restore the arrangement and try a follow shot. Finally, apply backspin to produce draw. Compare the cue ball's position after each shot and observe how its rotation changes the result.

title: Three Position Zones
text: Set up a shot with an object ball near a pocket. Choose three different areas where you'd like the cue ball to finish. Try to reach the first area using speed control, the second using follow or draw, and the third using a cushion route. Compare the difficulty and consistency of each approach.

title: First-session welcome
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Welcome to the Billiards Trainer. In the next few minutes, you'll learn how to aim a shot, adjust cue-ball movement, and plan more than one shot ahead. You can follow along with this short introduction or explore the trainer on your own. The guide will be here whenever you need it.

title: Executing your first shot
text: You're ready to try your first shot. Select Execute Shot and watch the shot. Notice how the object ball travels toward the pocket and where the cue ball finishes. This is the foundation of the trainer: make a decision, execute the shot, and study the result.

title: Introducing Shot 2
text: Shot 2 allows you to plan your next shot before executing the current one. Add a second planned cue ball and position it for the next object ball. You can adjust its aiming direction, speed, and spin while keeping your first shot ready.

title: Executing a two-shot sequence
text: With both shots planned, select Execute Shot. The trainer executes the first shot and advances to the second planned shot. That second cue ball becomes your active cue ball. You can examine its position, make adjustments, and select Execute Shot again when you're ready.

title: Extending the sequence
text: You aren't limited to planning only two shots. After executing a shot, the next planned cue ball becomes active. Before continuing, you can add another Shot 2. Repeat this process to plan and execute an entire runout, one shot at a time.

title: Discovering Undo Last Shot
text: One of the trainer's most useful features is Undo Last Shot. It allows you to step backward through your completed shots, even through a full rack. Return to an earlier shot, examine the position you created, and try a different approach. You can learn from the decisions you made without starting the entire layout over.

title: Completing the introduction
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: You've completed your introduction to the Billiards Trainer. You now know how to aim, adjust shot speed and spin, execute shots, plan ahead, and revisit earlier decisions. Continue exploring the table, or open the guide whenever you want to learn a new technique. Enjoy your practice.

title: Welcome to the Billiards Trainer
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Welcome to the Billiards Trainer. This interactive learning environment helps you explore shot geometry, cue-ball control, and the physics of billiards. Whether you're learning the fundamentals or improving advanced techniques, you can practice at your own pace and explore the results of different shots.

title: Learning at your own pace
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: You don't need to complete every lesson before using the trainer. Explore the table, experiment with shots, and open the guide whenever you want an explanation. You can return to any topic as often as you like.

title: Quick Help
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Quick Help provides a short explanation of a feature or technique. Use it when you want to understand a control without leaving your practice session. Each explanation focuses on what the feature does and how you can use it.

title: Advanced explanations
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Some topics include an advanced explanation that explores the underlying geometry, physics, or strategy in greater detail. Start with the quick explanation, then choose the advanced lesson whenever you want to understand more.

title: Learning by listening
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The guide includes spoken explanations so you can learn while looking at the table. Listen to a lesson, examine the visual guides, and experiment with the controls. You can also read the accompanying text whenever you prefer.

title: Learning by doing
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Many lessons include a practice exercise. After listening to an explanation, try the technique yourself. Adjust the shot, select Execute Shot, and observe the result. Repeating the exercise helps turn an explanation into a skill you can use.

title: Returning to the table
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: You can return to the table whenever you're ready to practice. The guide is there to support your learning, not interrupt it. Explore a topic, try the technique, and come back for more instruction whenever you need it.

title: Understanding a control
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: When you're unsure what a control does, open its explanation. The guide will describe its purpose and how it affects your shot. You can then return to the table and experiment with the control to see the difference.

title: Understanding the visual guides
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The trainer displays visual references to help you understand aiming, ball contact, and cue-ball movement. If a line or marker is unfamiliar, use the guide to learn what it represents. Understanding these visual references will help you interpret the shot.

title: Reviewing a lesson
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: You can revisit a lesson whenever you need a refresher. Review the explanation, listen again, or repeat the practice exercise. Learning a technique often takes several attempts, and you can return to it as many times as you like.

title: Audio playback controls
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: You can listen to a lesson whenever you're ready. Use the playback controls to pause, ree-ZOOM, or replay the explanation. You can also read the text without listening to the audio.

title: Choosing a learning level
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Start with Quick Help for a simple explanation. When you're ready to explore the technique in more detail, choose Advanced. Both levels cover the same subject, but the advanced lesson provides additional technical insight.

title: Contextual help
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: You can open help for the feature you're currently exploring. Whether you're adjusting shot speed, studying a tangent line, or planning a runout, the guide can explain that specific topic without requiring you to work through unrelated lessons.

title: Getting comfortable with the table
text: This is your practice table. You can position balls, explore aiming angles, and examine the paths they may take. The visual guides help you understand what happens when the cue ball contacts another ball. Start by looking at the cue ball and the object ball in front of you.

title: Aiming your first shot
text: Let's aim your first shot. Select a position on the table to change the cue ball's aiming direction. Watch how the aiming guides respond. If you're using a mouse, you can also use the scroll wheel for precise adjustments. Try aligning the shot toward the object ball.

title: Understanding the ghost ball
text: The ghost ball shows where the center of the cue ball needs to be when it contacts the object ball. It's a useful reference for understanding the correct aiming angle. Examine the ghost-ball position and adjust your aim until the object ball is directed toward the pocket.

title: Adjusting shot speed
text: Shot speed affects how the balls move and where the cue ball finishes. Find the speed control and try a small adjustment. For your first shot, use a moderate speed. Later, you'll explore how speed helps control your position for the next shot.

title: Changing the result
text: Now let's see how a small change affects the shot. Return to the starting arrangement and adjust the speed or aiming direction. Execute Shot again and compare the result. Experimenting with one change at a time is one of the best ways to understand what the cue ball is doing.

title: Introduction to follow and draw
text: Follow and draw help control the cue ball after contact. Follow adds forward rotation, while draw adds backspin. Try a straight shot using follow, then repeat it using draw. Watch how the cue ball behaves differently after striking the object ball.

title: Thinking about the next shot
text: Pocketing a ball is only part of the game. You also want to leave the cue ball in a good position for your next shot. Place two object balls on the table and decide which one you'll pocket first. Then consider where the cue ball should finish to make the second shot easier.

title: Contact & Aim
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Contact and Aim explains which ball the cue ball will hit first, the angle of that contact, and how much the balls overlap. Use it to check whether your aiming adjustment produces the contact you intended.

title: Cut angle
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Cut angle at contact describes how far the collision is from a straight-on hit. A zero-degree cut is straight on. Larger cut angles represent thinner contact between the balls.

title: Physical overlap
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Physical overlap shows how much the two balls overlap along the collision line. One hundred percent represents a full-ball hit. Smaller percentages indicate a thinner hit.

title: Travel to contact
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Cue-ball travel to contact shows the distance the cue ball travels before its predicted contact. The display expresses that distance in ball diameters, so you can compare short and long approaches.

title: Cue & Flight
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Cue and Flight describes the cue-tip contact and any predicted deviation or airborne behavior. This group becomes especially useful when experimenting with English, elevated cues, jumps, or mass-ay.

title: Predicted squirt
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Predicted cue-ball squirt shows the initial sideways deflection associated with off-center cue contact. Compare the value as you change left or right English, and watch how the aiming path responds.

title: Jump and clearance
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Jump and flight, obstacle clearance, and jump guide provide readings for elevated shots when applicable. Use them together to check whether the cue ball will rise, clear a blocking ball, and return to the cloth. A dash means the panel is not showing a result for that item in the current setup.

title: Curve and massé
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Curve and mass-ay describes predicted cue-ball curvature when your settings produce that type of shot. Compare the reading with the path drawn on the table as you adjust elevation, spin, and speed.

title: Power & Pocket
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Power and Pocket helps connect shot speed with ball travel. It includes a power feel reference, pocket speed, and speed readings for the cue ball and object ball.

title: Power feel and pocket speed
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: Power feel and pocket speed provide references for how strongly the shot is set and how the object ball will approach the pocket. Use the diamond and lag references to compare shot strength and pocket speed.

title: Ball speeds
decision: Concept, interface explanation, or session guidance; no prescribed starting ball arrangement
text: The cue-ball-to-object-ball speed row displays speed readings associated with the approach and collision, while the object-ball-to-pocket row shows the ball speed toward the pocket. Values shown in meters per second help you compare ball speeds. Interpret them alongside friction, cut angle, and the resulting ball path.

title: Live adjustment
text: Set up a straight shot and open Live Stats. Notice the cut angle and physical overlap. Move the aim slightly to create a thinner contact, then watch both readings change. Return to a full-ball hit and compare the paths before selecting Execute Shot.

title: Speed and spin
text: Set up a repeatable shot and open Live Stats. First adjust shot speed and compare the power and ball-speed predictions. Then restore the starting setup, change left or right English, and examine predicted squirt. Change only one setting at a time so the differences are easier to understand.

title: Practice pathway
text: Start with cue ball speed and contact, then target landing, pattern play, and kick routes. Finish with a scored benchmark. Open More for the matching video. Watch the creator demonstrate the layout, then build your own practice table. Save a starting layout before changing it so you can repeat the same test. Count pocketing, cue ball position, and legal contact separately. Your score should show what improved and what still needs work.

title: Speed and contact baseline
text: Begin with a straight shot and center cue tip contact. Find the speed that produces a stop shot, then move the contact point higher for follow and lower for draw. Keep the object ball and pocket fixed while changing one setting at a time. Next, use a cut shot to compare the tangent line with the cue ball route. Before each shot, name the landing point you expect. Repeat each setup five times and record whether the cue ball finished short, long, left, or right.

title: Target landing precision
text: Set up a repeatable object ball shot and choose a small cue ball landing zone. Begin with a generous target, then reduce it as your control improves. For this practice plan, use a three inch target and count a success only when the object ball is pocketed and the cue ball center finishes inside the target. Shoot ten attempts. Change only speed, then contact height, then the cut angle. Aim for eight successes out of ten before making the target smaller. Open More for Dr. Dave’s target practice demonstration.

title: Rock Around the Clock
text: Open More and use Niels Feijen’s demonstration to set up Rock Around the Clock. Save the starting layout. Before every shot, choose the next object ball, its pocket, and the cue ball landing zone that leaves a useful angle. Prefer a route with room for a small speed error. Track pocketing and position separately. Complete one rotation first, then work toward three consecutive rotations without disturbing another ball. When you miss position, repeat the previous shot and compare a simpler route before changing the whole pattern.

title: One-rail kick reference
text: Place an object ball behind a blocker so the cue ball needs one cushion to reach it. Open More for the diamond system tutorial. Identify the cue ball start, the rail aim point, and the intended object ball contact. Keep speed and spin consistent while testing the route. Repeat five attempts, moving the rail aim point by a small amount when the contact misses. Record the adjustment that works, then test a second starting location. Count legal object ball contact according to the game you are practicing.

title: Two-rail kick extension
text: Begin with a two cushion route that has space for the cue ball to travel. Mark the first rail aim point and predict the second rail contact before shooting. Keep the same speed and spin for each attempt. If the first contact is wrong, adjust the aim point. If the first contact is right but the final contact misses, examine the second rail route and speed. Record five attempts from the same start, then move the cue ball to a new starting diamond. Open More for the linked kick reference.

title: Corner-5 three-rail route
text: Open More for Dr. Dave’s Corner-5 demonstration. Follow its starting, aiming, and arrival number scales together. Identify all three cushion contacts before you shoot. Start with a clear route, consistent speed, and the spin shown in the lesson. Compare the predicted arrival with the actual arrival, then make a small adjustment and repeat. Once the route is calibrated, add a target object ball and a blocker for escape practice. Test five different starting positions and record legal object ball contact separately from the final cue ball position.

title: Progressive difficulty benchmark
text: Open More for Sharivari’s progressive difficulty drill and use the demonstrated setup. Save the starting layout and record your first score. For your Trainer adaptation, begin with a comfortable position zone. After a successful set, reduce the zone or increase the shot difficulty, changing one condition at a time. Count both the pocketed ball and the required cue ball position. If the same error repeats, return to the last successful level. Record the highest level you can repeat, rather than only your best isolated attempt.

title: 105-minute practice session
text: Use this one hundred and five minute practice plan. Spend thirty minutes on speed and target landing, aiming for eight successful pocket and position results out of ten with a three inch target. Spend forty five minutes on Rock Around the Clock, first completing one rotation and then working toward three consecutive rotations without disturbing another ball. Spend thirty minutes on kick escapes, starting with one rail and adding two and three rails as control improves. Test five selected escapes and aim for four legal contacts. Record the result at the end of each phase. If time runs out, save your layout and score, then continue there next session.

title: Review, save, and repeat
text: At the end of practice, record attempts, pocketed balls, successful position results, and legal kick contacts. Note the most common miss and the single adjustment that helped. Save the table with a name that includes the drill, difficulty, and date. Download its table file if you want to share the same layout with an instructor or student. Begin your next session with that saved layout and the same scoring conditions. Improve the weakest result first, then increase the challenge once you can repeat the improvement.

title: Tor Lowry and Zero-X Billiards
text: We’ve found Tor Lowry’s Zero X Billiards videos helpful in advancing our games, and we recommend them as a companion to your practice in the Trainer. His lessons cover fundamentals, cue ball control, position play, patterns, and defense. Choose a topic that matches what you are practicing. Watch the demonstration, then recreate a manageable layout in the Trainer. Open More for the official channel and training resources.

title: Zero-X: center-ball fundamentals
text: We’ve found Tor Lowry’s center ball lessons helpful for improving pocketing and cue ball control, and we recommend them for building a dependable foundation. Start with the vertical center line, then explore stop, follow, and draw without adding side spin. Keep the same layout and change one setting at a time. Watch his demonstration before practicing, and compare your expected landing point with the result. Open More for Zero X’s official lessons.

title: Zero-X: position play
text: We’ve found Tor Lowry’s position play lessons helpful in advancing our games, particularly when planning how one shot prepares the next. We recommend watching for the intended angle, cue ball route, and landing area. Pause the demonstration and plan the next position yourself. In the Trainer, use Shot 2 to compare routes, then save the layout and repeat the approach that gives you more room for error. Open More for the Zero X resources.

title: Zero-X: eight-ball patterns
text: We’ve found Tor Lowry’s eight ball pattern lessons helpful in improving our planning through a full rack, and we recommend them when individual shots feel comfortable but the runout becomes difficult. Study the order of play, the useful angles, and how problems are addressed before they restrict your choices. Begin with a small group of balls in the Trainer and plan a clear route through them. Save the starting layout to compare different patterns. Open More for the Zero X lessons.

title: Zero-X: defense and recovery
text: We’ve found Tor Lowry’s defensive lessons helpful in advancing our games, especially when a shot leaves us without ideal position. We recommend studying how cue ball control and ball placement can limit an opponent’s options. Recreate a simple situation in the Trainer and compare an attacking route with a defensive route. Judge both the object ball result and the position you leave. Open More for Zero X’s official lessons on defense and related skills.

title: Stop Shot Calibration
text: Stop Shot Calibration. Stand at the head end, looking toward the foot end. Place the 1-ball on the center spot. Put the cue ball on the head string, one diamond from the left long rail. This lines up with the foot-right corner pocket. Center a three-inch white circle one ball width behind the 1-ball, toward the cue ball. That is the cue ball’s stopping position. Use no side spin. Start slightly below center and adjust your speed and tip height until the cue ball arrives without forward or backward roll. Pocket the 1-ball and stop the cue ball inside the white circle. Reset both balls after each attempt. Try five shots and count clean stops. In the Trainer, select Execute Shot to watch the result.

title: 90-Degree Stun Tangent Line
text: Ninety-Degree Stun Tangent Line. Stand at the head end, looking toward the foot. Place the 1-ball one diamond inward from the right side pocket. Put the cue ball on the table’s center line, half a diamond toward the foot end from the center spot. Place a three-inch yellow square one and a half diamonds toward the head end from the 1-ball, and one ball width to its left. Pocket the 1-ball into the right side pocket. Use no side spin and enough low tip contact and speed for the cue ball to be sliding at impact. It should leave along the tangent line, perpendicular to the object ball’s path. Adjust speed to finish inside the yellow square. Reset both balls and repeat five times. Select Execute Shot in the Trainer to compare the path with the tangent line.

title: Speed Ladder — Four Zones
text: Speed Ladder. Stand at the head end, looking toward the foot. Use only the cue ball. Start on the center line, half a diamond behind the head string. Place four three-inch circles on the center line: white on the center spot, red on the foot spot, yellow one diamond from the foot cushion, and pink one diamond from the head cushion. Reset the cue ball to the same starting position before every shot. First, stop on white. Second, stop on red. Third, touch the foot cushion and return to yellow. Fourth, touch the foot cushion and return all the way to pink. Use a level cue and no side spin. Change your stroke speed while keeping your delivery smooth. Score one point for each finish inside its circle, for a maximum of four. Repeat the ladder and compare your scores.

title: L-Drill — Five-Ball Rotation
text: The L-Drill. Stand at the head end, looking toward the foot. Place balls one, two, and three half a diamond from the right long rail, respectively one, two, and three diamonds from the foot cushion. Place ball four one diamond from the right long rail and half a diamond from the foot cushion. Place ball five on the center line, also half a diamond from the foot cushion. These five balls form an L. Put a white square at the center spot, one diamond wide. Start the cue ball on the center line, half a diamond behind the head string. Pocket balls one through five in order, choosing clear corner pockets. Plan the next angle before every shot. Use the center square as a recovery option when it helps the next shot. Count balls pocketed in sequence, then reset the full pattern and try again.

title: T-Drill — Center and Foot String
text: The T-Drill. Stand at the head end, looking toward the foot. Place ball one on the center spot. Place ball two one diamond farther toward the foot, and ball three on the foot spot. Put ball four on the foot string, one diamond to the left of ball three, and ball five one diamond to its right. Start the cue ball on the head string, one diamond from the right long rail. Place two yellow circles, each half a diamond wide, halfway between the center spot and the side pockets. Pocket balls one through five in order into corner pockets. Choose the yellow zone that gives you a useful angle for the next ball. Use a cushion when it helps the route. Keep the cue ball clear of the remaining balls. Count your run, reset the full pattern, and work toward completing all five.

title: Wagon Wheel — Six Target Zones
text: The Wagon Wheel. Stand at the head end, looking toward the foot. Place the 1-ball one diamond inward from the right side pocket. Put the cue ball on the center line, half a diamond toward the foot from the center spot. Set six three-inch circles on the head side of the 1-ball. Marker one is one and a half diamonds from the left rail and three and a half from the head rail. Marker two is two from the left and three from the head. Marker three is one ball width left of the 1-ball’s line and three from the head. Marker four is three and a quarter from the left and three from the head. Marker five is three and a half from the left and two and a half from the head. Marker six is directly headward of marker three, one and a half diamonds from the head rail. Reset both balls before every attempt and pocket the 1-ball into the right side pocket. Work through the markers in order, varying draw, follow, and speed. Start without side spin. Record the combinations that produce repeatable finishes.

title: Two-Rail Center Recovery
text: Two-Rail Center Recovery. Stand at the head end, looking toward the foot. Place the 1-ball one diamond from the right long rail and one diamond from the foot cushion. Put the cue ball on the same rail offset, three diamonds from the foot cushion. Place a white square on the center line, one diamond from the head cushion. Make the square one diamond wide. Pocket the 1-ball into the foot-right corner. Start with natural forward roll and no side spin. Look for the cue ball to contact the foot cushion, then the left long cushion, and travel toward the white recovery zone. Adjust your stroke speed to finish in the square. Keep the ball placements fixed so you can compare attempts. Score the pocketed ball and the position result separately. Try five shots, then repeat your most successful speed.

title: Side Pocket Scratch Avoidance
text: Side Pocket Scratch Avoidance. Stand at the head end, looking toward the foot. Place the 1-ball half a diamond inward from the right side pocket. Start the cue ball on the foot spot. Place a red square beside the head-right corner pocket, centered a quarter diamond from each cushion. Make it half a diamond wide. Place a white square on the center line, one diamond from the foot cushion, and make it one diamond wide. Pocket the 1-ball into the right side pocket. Compare forward roll, stun, and controlled draw, starting without side spin. Watch the whole cue ball route, including any cushion rebounds. Find a stroke that keeps the cue ball clear of the red danger zone and returns it toward white. In the Trainer, judge whether the path enters the red zone, even if cue ball pocketing is prevented. Reset both balls and repeat five times.

title: One-Rail Mirror Kick
text: One-Rail Mirror Kick. Stand at the head end, looking toward the foot. Put the cue ball on the head string, one diamond from the right long rail. Place the 1-ball on that same line, three diamonds from the foot cushion. Put the 8-ball halfway between them to block the direct shot. The cue ball and the 1-ball are now equally distant from the left cushion. Mark the left cushion halfway between their lengthwise positions: three and a half diamonds from the head cushion. Center a yellow circle one ball radius inside that cushion as the cue ball contact reference. Use a level cue, moderate speed, and no side spin. Send the cue ball to the left cushion, then into the 1-ball without touching the 8-ball first. Begin with the midpoint reference and make small aiming adjustments from your observed results. Reset the cue ball after each attempt and count five clean contacts.

title: Two-Rail Corner Kick
text: Two-Rail Corner Kick. Stand at the head end, looking toward the foot. Place the cue ball one diamond from the head cushion and one and a quarter diamonds from the right long rail. Put the 1-ball one diamond from the foot cushion and three quarters of a diamond from the right long rail. Place the 8-ball level with the side pockets, one diamond from the right rail. Put balls two and three on the same line, two ball widths to either side of the 8-ball toward the head and foot ends. This blocks the direct shot. Place yellow marker A at the right cushion on the foot string, with its center one ball radius inside the cloth. Place yellow marker B half a diamond left of the foot-right corner, also one ball radius inside the foot cushion. Use moderate speed and no side spin. Aim the cue ball center toward A. Look for right cushion, then foot cushion near B, then contact with the 1-ball. Make small aiming adjustments and count five successful escapes.
